questions.stem: Why are giant covalent structures solids with high melting points?

options.text: Many strong covalent bonds run through the whole structure and need lots of energy to overcome
options.explanation: Melting must disrupt the bonded network itself, and the bonds are strong, so the energy cost is huge.

options.text: Their molecules are very large and heavy
options.explanation: There are no separate molecules in a giant structure; the bonding network is continuous.
options.misconception: molecular picture applied to a giant lattice

options.text: The atoms are held by weak forces that take time to overcome
options.explanation: The forces involved are strong covalent bonds, not weak intermolecular forces.

options.text: Their high melting points come from metallic bonding
options.explanation: Giant covalent structures contain non-metals bonded covalently; metallic bonding belongs to metals.

questions.stem: What alternative names are used for giant covalent structures?

options.text: Giant lattices, or macromolecules
options.explanation: Both names appear of record: the structure is a giant lattice, and the exam hint adds macromolecule.

options.text: Simple molecules
options.explanation: Simple molecular structures are the opposite case: small separate molecules with weak forces between them.

options.text: Ionic lattices
options.explanation: Ionic lattices hold charged ions; giant covalent structures hold neutral atoms bonded covalently.

options.text: Metallic lattices
options.explanation: Metallic lattices describe metals with delocalised electrons, not covalent networks of non-metals.

questions.stem: What is fixed about the ratio of atoms in a giant covalent structure?

options.text: The bonded network repeats with a fixed ratio of atoms in the overall structure
options.explanation: Each repeat unit contains the same atom ratio, which the network then extends uniformly.

options.text: The ratio changes as the crystal grows larger
options.explanation: Growth extends the same repeating pattern; the ratio stays fixed throughout.

options.text: The ratio is always one atom to one atom
options.explanation: Ratios vary by substance; the point is that the ratio is fixed, not that it equals one-to-one.

options.text: Only the surface atoms follow a ratio
options.explanation: The fixed ratio governs the whole network, not just its boundary.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances are the standard examples of giant covalent structures?

options.text: Diamond and graphite
options.explanation: Both are carbon allotropes whose covalent bonding extends through the entire solid.

options.text: Oxygen and water
options.explanation: Both are simple molecular substances with weak forces between small molecules.

options.text: Sodium chloride and magnesium oxide
options.explanation: Both are ionic compounds with giant ionic lattices, not covalent networks.

options.text: Copper and zinc
options.explanation: Both are metals with metallic bonding and delocalised electrons.

questions.stem: A giant covalent structure and a simple molecular substance both contain covalent bonds. Why do their melting points differ so much?

options.text: Melting the giant structure must break covalent bonds throughout the network, while the molecular substance only overcomes weak forces between molecules
options.explanation: The energy gap comes from what melting attacks: a continuous bonded network versus weak intermolecular forces.

options.text: The molecular substance has stronger covalent bonds
options.explanation: Covalent bonds are strong in both; the difference lies in what melting must overcome.

options.text: The giant structure is held by ionic attractions
options.explanation: The giant structure is covalently bonded; no ionic attractions are involved.

options.text: The molecular substance melts lower because its molecules are charged
options.explanation: The molecules are neutral; their low melting points follow from weak intermolecular forces.

questions.stem: Describe the melting behaviour and the building blocks of substances with giant covalent structures.
questions.modelAnswer: They are solids that melt at high temperatures, built from huge numbers of non-metal atoms bonded to other non-metal atoms.

questions.stem: Name the two standard examples of giant covalent structures given in the note.
questions.modelAnswer: Diamond and graphite are the two standard examples of giant covalent structures.

questions.stem: Explain why a giant covalent structure has a high melting point, referring to the bonds that must be overcome.
questions.modelAnswer: High melting points follow because the strong covalent bonds run throughout the whole structure, and those bonds need lots of energy to overcome before the solid melts.

questions.stem: A data booklet lists a solid as a 'giant lattice' of one non-metal element with a fixed atom ratio. Using the vocabulary of record, classify its structure type and state what is fixed about its composition.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a giant covalent structure, also called a giant lattice; the ratio of atoms overall is fixed, even though huge numbers of atoms are bonded together.

options.text: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others by very strong covalent bonds in a rigid network
options.explanation: The four-bonded network leaves no weak direction, so the crystal resists scratching and cutting.

options.text: Its layers slide over each other under pressure
options.explanation: Sliding layers describe graphite; diamond has no such planes.

options.text: Its carbon atoms are unusually heavy
options.explanation: All carbon atoms are identical; hardness follows the bonding, not the mass.

options.text: It contains metallic bonds that resist damage
options.explanation: Diamond is covalently bonded throughout; no metallic bonding is present.

questions.stem: Why can graphite conduct electricity, while diamond cannot?

options.text: Graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon that moves along its layers, while diamond's four-bonded carbons leave no electrons free
options.explanation: The fourth outer electron in graphite is unbonded and mobile; diamond uses all four in bonds.

options.text: Graphite's bonds are weaker, so electrons escape
options.explanation: Conduction follows from delocalised electrons, not from broken or weak bonds.

options.text: Diamond's electrons are negative, while graphite's are positive
options.explanation: Electrons are negative in every substance; the difference is mobility.

options.text: Diamond conducts only when molten
options.explanation: Diamond's network has no mobile electrons in any state at this level.

questions.stem: Why is graphite soft and slippery?

options.text: Its layers slide over each other because only weak forces act between the layers
options.explanation: The strong bonds lie within each hexagonal layer; between layers the forces are weak, so planes slip.

options.text: Its carbon atoms are joined by weak covalent bonds
options.explanation: The covalent bonds within each layer are strong; the weakness lies between the layers.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons push the layers apart
options.explanation: The electrons enable conduction; sliding follows from weak inter-layer forces.

options.text: It melts at room temperature into a slippery liquid
options.explanation: Graphite is a high-melting solid; its slipperiness belongs to the solid itself.

questions.stem: Diamond is described as hard but is it the strongest material?

options.text: No: hard describes resistance to scratching, and diamond is brittle enough to be smashed
options.explanation: The exam hint separates the two words: diamond is the hardest natural mineral, yet brittle under a hammer blow.

options.text: Yes, hardness and strength are the same property
options.explanation: The two words mean different things here; hardness resists scratching, strength resists breaking apart.

options.text: No, because diamond melts too easily to be strong
options.explanation: Diamond has a very high melting point; its brittleness, not its melting point, separates it from strength.

options.text: Yes, because its bonds cannot be broken at all
options.explanation: Its bonds are strong but breakable; no bond is unbreakable.

questions.stem: Pencil lead is often said to contain lead. What is the truth of record at this level?

options.text: Pencil lead is graphite, with nothing in common with the metal lead
options.explanation: The writing material is graphite, whose layers flake onto the page; the metal lead is unrelated.

options.text: It is a soft alloy of lead and graphite
options.explanation: No lead enters the pencil core; the name is purely historical.

options.text: It is diamond dust in a binder
options.explanation: Diamond is the hard allotrope; pencils need the soft, flaking layers of graphite.

options.text: It is pure carbon in the fullerene form
options.explanation: Pencil marks come from layered graphite, not from buckyball fullerene.

questions.stem: State the term for substances made of the same carbon atoms arranged in different bonding patterns, and name the two in this note.
questions.modelAnswer: They are allotropes: diamond and graphite are both made of carbon atoms arranged in different bonding patterns.

questions.stem: State how many other carbon atoms each carbon bonds to in graphite, and what structure those bonds build.
questions.modelAnswer: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, forming layers of hexagons, and one electron per atom is left free.

questions.stem: Explain why graphite is soft and slippery, and why it conducts electricity, in terms of its layers and electrons.
questions.modelAnswer: Graphite is soft and slippery because its layers slide over each other, and it conducts because its delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure.

questions.stem: A workshop needs a material to cut through stone. Using diamond's bonding arrangement, justify which property makes it suitable and link it to its structure.
questions.modelAnswer: Diamond is very hard, which makes it useful for cutting tools; the hardness follows from each carbon bonding to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement with very strong bonds.
